answer_text:
Let \(T:V\to V\) be differentiation, so

\[
T(p(x))=p'(x),
\]

where \(V=\{p(x)\in F[x]: \deg p\le n\}\).

Suppose \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\). Then there is a nonzero polynomial \(p(x)\in V\) such that

\[
p'(x)=\lambda p(x).
\]

We check whether \(\lambda\neq 0\) is possible.

Let \(d=\deg p\). Since \(p\neq 0\), either \(d=0\) or \(d\ge 1\).

- If \(d=0\), then \(p(x)=c\) is a nonzero constant. Then

\[
p'(x)=0.
\]

So the eigenvalue equation becomes

\[
0=\lambda c.
\]

If \(\lambda\neq 0\), then \(c=0\), contradicting \(p\neq 0\). Thus no nonzero constant gives a nonzero eigenvalue.

- If \(d\ge 1\), then

\[
\deg(\lambda p)=d
\]

whenever \(\lambda\neq 0\). But differentiation lowers degree by at least \(1\), so

\[
\deg(p')\le d-1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\deg(p') < \deg(\lambda p),
\]

which makes the identity \(p'=\lambda p\) impossible.

Hence no nonzero polynomial satisfies \(p'=\lambda p\) when \(\lambda\neq 0\). On the other hand, every nonzero constant polynomial satisfies

\[
T(c)=0,
\]

so \(\lambda=0\) is indeed an eigenvalue.

Thus the differentiation operator on \(V\) has no eigenvalues other than \(0\).

\[
\boxed{\text{No, the only eigenvalue is }0.}
\]
